entities.summary:
Theuderic II, king of Burgundy (595–613) and Austrasia (612–613), was the second son of Childebert II. At his father's death in 595, he received Guntram's kingdom of Burgundy, with its capital at Orléans, while his elder brother, Theudebert II, received their father's kingdom of Austrasia, with its capital at Metz. He also received the lordship of the cities (civitates) of Toulouse, Agen, Nantes, Angers, Saintes, Angoulême, Périgueux, Blois, Chartres, and Le Mans. Theuderic II played a crucial role in the Salian Franks' expansion into the Frankish territories, and his reign saw the rise of the Merovingian dynasty. He was succeeded by his brother Theudebert II, who continued the expansion of the Frankish kingdom. Theuderic II's death in 613 CE marked the end of the Salian Franks' territorial expansion, but his legacy as a key figure in the rise of the Merovingian dynasty endured.

Theuderic II's reign was marked by military campaigns and strategic alliances, which led to the expansion of the Frankish kingdom. He formed alliances with the Alamanni and the Saxons, which helped to secure the borders of the kingdom. His military campaigns also led to the capture of several strategic cities, including Toulouse and Agen, which became key centers of power for the Merovingian dynasty.

Theuderic II's legacy can be seen in the continuation of the Merovingian dynasty, which ruled the Frankish kingdom for centuries. His brother Theudebert II continued to expand the kingdom, and the Merovingian dynasty played a significant role in shaping the course of European history. Theuderic II's reign also saw the rise of the Catholic Church, which became a powerful force in the Frankish kingdom. He was a key figure in the conversion of the Salian Franks to Christianity, and his reign marked the beginning of the Catholic Church's influence on European politics and society.
